# An all-dimensional section-product bound with an exact entropy deficit

Let Y_0,...,Y_d be independent unit-rate exponentials, d>=1, and let c have at least one positive and one negative coordinate. Put V=sum c_iY_i, let f=f_V(0)>0, and let b be the barycentric centroid of the proper simplex section c dot xi=0. Then, for every j with c_j!=0,

    d^d product_(i!=j) b_i >= |c_j| f.              (1)

The precise deficit is a nonnegative relative entropy, specified below. This is weaker than the proposed cap-variance bound F(1-F)<=d^d product_(i!=j)b_i. In particular it does not replace that unproved all-dimensional inequality.

## 1. The actual conditional law and its means

The conditional law at V=0 is defined by its coarea density. Fix j with c_j!=0, put z=(Y_i)_(i!=j), and eliminate

    Y_j=-sum_(i!=j)(c_i/c_j)z_i.

Its domain and density in the other d coordinates are

    C={z>=0: sum_(i!=j)(c_i/c_j)z_i<=0},
    p(z)=exp(-beta dot z)1_C(z)/Z,
    beta_i=1-c_i/c_j,
    Z=|c_j| f.                                    (2)

The factor |c_j| in Z is the exact coarea factor from integrating the delta constraint in Y_j. On C one has beta dot z=sum_i Y_i>=sum_(i!=j)z_i, so all required integrals and first moments are finite, even if a coefficient beta_i outside this cone is negative. The cone has nonempty interior because some c_i has sign opposite c_j. Therefore Z and every conditional mean mu_i=E_p z_i are strictly positive.

These conditional means are exactly

    mu_i=d b_i.                                    (3)

For completeness, write Y=G Xi with G Gamma(d+1,1) independent of uniform Xi on Delta_d. Conditioning G(c dot Xi)=0 weights the gamma density by 1/G, so its conditional density is Gamma(d,1), independent of uniform section measure. Thus E(G|V=0)=d and E(Xi_i|V=0)=b_i. Equivalently the same conclusion follows by the radial coarea parametrization of the cone over the section. This proves (3), including zero or repeated coefficients elsewhere in c.

## 2. Exact entropy identity

Since C is a cone, scaling its integral gives Z(s beta)=s^(-d)Z(beta) for s>0. Differentiating at s=1, justified by beta dot z>=sum z and exponential domination, gives

    sum_i beta_i mu_i=d.                           (4)

Let q be the product of independent exponential densities with the same means mu_i:

    q(z)=product_i mu_i^(-1) exp(-z_i/mu_i), z>=0.

On C, direct integration of the log density ratio gives

    D_KL(p||q)=int_C p log(p/q)
             =log[(product_i mu_i)/Z]
                -sum_i beta_i mu_i+sum_i E_p(z_i)/mu_i
             =log[(product_i mu_i)/Z].             (5)

All terms are finite by the preceding moment bounds. Nonnegativity follows without an external entropy theorem: with u=q/p on C, the elementary inequality log u<=u-1 gives

    -D_KL(p||q)=int_C p log(q/p)
       <=int_C q-1<=0.

Equations (2)--(5) prove (1), with the exact identity

    log[d^d product_(i!=j)b_i/(|c_j|f)]
       =D_KL(p||q)>=0.                             (6)

## 3. Equality and scope

If c_i/c_j<=0 for all i!=j, the cone C is the entire orthant, the beta_i are positive, and p is itself a product of exponentials. Thus equality holds in (1).

If some c_i/c_j>0, an open subset of the positive orthant is outside C. The product density q assigns that subset positive mass, so int_C q<1 and the displayed logarithm inequality makes D_KL(p||q)>0. Consequently (1) is strict. This exactly characterizes equality: the selected nonzero raw coefficient is the only coefficient of its sign, apart from arbitrary zero coefficients.

The factor |c_j|f is invariant under common positive scaling of c, as required for an ordinary section statement. The bound is not asserted for c_j=0 by division; its limit gives only the trivial lower bound zero.

To see why (1) does not by itself prove the cap-variance conjecture, take c=(1,1,-R) with R>0. Its captured probability and exponential density are

    F=(2R+1)/(R+1)^2,  f=R/(R+1)^2.

For R=10, F(1-F)=2100/14641>1210/14641=f. Thus replacing F(1-F) by |c_j|f at a positive coefficient j would lose exactly the entropy payment that must still be proved. The present note establishes an actual conditional-law identity and a precise nonnegative deficit, not the missing comparison between that deficit and the two cap probabilities.

## 4. Exact failure of a simple phase-merging monotonicity

A prospective induction might merge two coefficients of the same sign, preserving their sum and replacing the second by zero. Even the natural all-coordinate ratio

    R(c)=[product_(i=0)^d E(Y_i|V=0)]/[F(1-F)]

is not monotone in either fixed direction under this operation. Two exact tetrahedral examples suffice.

For c=(1,1,-1,-1), the conditional means are all 3/4 and F=1/2, so R=81/64. After merging to (1,1,-2,0), the means are (2/3,2/3,2/3,1), F=5/9, and R=6/5<81/64.

For c=(1,3,-1,-1), the actual quadrilateral centroid formulas give conditional means (7/10,2/5,19/20,19/20) and F=23/32. Thus R=161728/129375. After the same merge, c=(1,3,-2,0) has conditional means (2/3,2/5,14/15,1) and F=11/15. Its ratio is 14/11, which is larger by exactly 32242/1423125.

For the merged vectors these formulas follow directly by eliminating the single negative phase: for raw (p,q,-R,0), its zero-coordinate exponential remains independent with mean one, while the other conditional means are R/(p+R), R/(q+R), p/(p+R)+q/(q+R), and F=1-R^2/[(p+R)(q+R)]. All cuts are proper, and every displayed mean is an actual conditional mean. Hence an induction based on unconditional monotonicity of this phase merge would require a new argument or an additional hypothesis.
